concepts.title: Rubber Sheet Geometry
concepts.contentHtml:
Topology studies properties of shapes that survive continuous deformation -- stretching, bending, squishing -- but not tearing or gluing.

A circle and a square are topologically the same: you can smoothly reshape one into the other.

But a circle and a figure-eight are different: you'd have to cut or glue to transform one into the other.

concepts.title: Homeomorphism
concepts.contentHtml:
Two shapes are homeomorphic (topologically equivalent) if one can be continuously deformed into the other.

The classic joke: a topologist can't tell the difference between a coffee mug and a donut. Both have exactly one hole!

Homeomorphism is the topological version of "same shape" -- it preserves connectivity, holes, and boundaries.

concepts.title: Open and Closed Sets
concepts.contentHtml:
An open set doesn't include its boundary -- like an open disc (all points less than 1 from the center, but not the circle itself).

A closed set includes its boundary -- like a closed disc (including the circle).

These concepts are fundamental to topology. A topology on a set is essentially a choice of which subsets to call "open."

concepts.title: The Zoo of Surfaces
concepts.contentHtml:
Sphere: The surface of a ball. No holes, no edges.

Torus: The surface of a donut. One hole through the middle.

Möbius strip: A strip with a twist -- has only one side and one edge!

Klein bottle: Like a Möbius strip but closed into a tube -- has no inside or outside. Can't exist in 3D without self-intersection.

concepts.title: Orientability
concepts.contentHtml:
A surface is orientable if it has two distinct sides (an inside and an outside).

Imagine an ant walking on a Möbius strip. It walks all the way around and ends up on the "other side" without ever crossing an edge. The strip has only one side!

The sphere and torus are orientable. The Möbius strip and Klein bottle are non-orientable.

concepts.title: Genus: Counting Holes
concepts.contentHtml:
The genus of a surface is the number of "handles" or holes it has.

Sphere: genus 0 (no holes)
Torus: genus 1 (one hole)
Double torus: genus 2 (two holes)

The remarkable Classification Theorem says every closed orientable surface is determined by its genus. There's one surface for each genus!
mathExpressions: g = 0 \rightarrow S^2, \quad g = 1 \rightarrow T^2, \quad g = 2 \rightarrow T^2 \# T^2

concepts.title: Euler's Formula for Polyhedra
concepts.contentHtml:
Take any convex polyhedron (like a cube or tetrahedron). Count its vertices (V), edges (E), and faces (F).

No matter which polyhedron you pick:

V - E + F = 2

This is Euler's polyhedron formula. Try it on a cube: 8 - 12 + 6 = 2. A tetrahedron: 4 - 6 + 4 = 2. It always works!

concepts.title: Euler Characteristic for Surfaces
concepts.contentHtml:
The Euler characteristic χ generalizes beyond polyhedra to any surface.

For a surface of genus g (with g holes):

χ = 2 - 2g

Sphere (g=0): χ = 2
Torus (g=1): χ = 0
Double torus (g=2): χ = -2

This single number captures deep topological information!

concepts.title: Why It's Topological
concepts.contentHtml:
The Euler characteristic is a topological invariant -- it doesn't change when you deform the surface.

You can subdivide a cube into smaller faces, adding vertices and edges, and χ still equals 2.

This means χ is a tool for proving two surfaces are not equivalent: if they have different χ, they can't be homeomorphic!

concepts.title: What is a Mathematical Knot?
concepts.contentHtml:
A mathematical knot is a closed loop in 3D space -- imagine tying a knot in a rope, then fusing the ends together.

The simplest knot is the unknot -- just a plain circle, no crossings.

The trefoil knot is the simplest non-trivial knot: it has 3 crossings and can't be untangled.

concepts.title: Reidemeister Moves
concepts.contentHtml:
Two knot diagrams represent the same knot if you can get from one to the other using three types of moves:

Type I: Add or remove a twist (loop)
Type II: Add or remove two crossings by sliding one strand over another
Type III: Slide a strand over a crossing

If two diagrams are connected by these moves, the knots are equivalent.

concepts.title: Knot Invariants
concepts.contentHtml:
How do you prove two knots are different? You need a knot invariant -- a property that doesn't change under Reidemeister moves.

Crossing number: The minimum number of crossings in any diagram of the knot. Unknot = 0, trefoil = 3, figure-eight = 4.

Tricolorability: Can you color the strands with 3 colors following certain rules? The trefoil is tricolorable; the unknot is not -- so they're different knots!

concepts.title: Paths and Loops
concepts.contentHtml:
A path in a space is a continuous curve from point A to point B. A loop is a path that starts and ends at the same point.

Two loops are considered "the same" if one can be continuously deformed into the other (this is called homotopy).

On a plane, every loop can be shrunk to a point. But on a torus, a loop that goes "around the hole" can never be shrunk — the hole blocks it.

concepts.title: The Fundamental Group π₁
concepts.contentHtml:
The fundamental group π₁(X) of a space X is the set of all loops (up to homotopy) with the operation of concatenation (walk the first loop, then the second).

This is one of the most powerful topological invariants — it captures the "hole structure" of a space algebraically.

Examples:

π₁(disk) = {e} (trivial — no holes)
π₁(circle) = ℤ (the integers — loops counted by winding number)
π₁(torus) = ℤ × ℤ (two independent loops)

concepts.title: Simply Connected Spaces
concepts.contentHtml:
A space is simply connected if every loop can be shrunk to a point — i.e., π₁ = {e}.

Examples: the sphere, Euclidean space, a disk. Not simply connected: the circle, the torus, the figure-eight.

The famous Poincaré Conjecture (proved by Perelman in 2003) states: the only simply connected, closed 3-manifold is the 3-sphere. This was one of the Millennium Prize Problems!

concepts.title: What is Compactness?
concepts.contentHtml:
Compactness is the topological generalization of being "closed and bounded." It captures the idea that a space is "finite" in a topological sense.

Formal definition: a space is compact if every open cover has a finite subcover. (If you cover it with possibly infinitely many open sets, you can always pick finitely many that still cover it.)

Think of it as: compact spaces have no way to escape to infinity.

concepts.title: The Heine-Borel Theorem
concepts.contentHtml:
In ℝⁿ, compactness has a beautifully simple characterization:

Heine-Borel: A subset of ℝⁿ is compact if and only if it is closed and bounded.

Compact: [0,1], a closed disk, a sphere
Not compact: (0,1) (not closed), ℝ (not bounded), {1/n : n≥1} (not closed)

This theorem only works in ℝⁿ. In general topological spaces, compact is a much subtler notion.

concepts.title: Why Compactness Matters
concepts.contentHtml:
Compactness is the key hypothesis in many powerful theorems:

Extreme Value Theorem: A continuous function on a compact set achieves its maximum and minimum. (This is why we can always optimize on a compact domain!)

Uniform continuity: Continuous functions on compact sets are uniformly continuous.

Sequential compactness: In metric spaces, compact means every sequence has a convergent subsequence — you can't "drift away."
mathExpressions: f : K \to \mathbb{R} \text{ continuous, } K \text{ compact} \implies f \text{ achieves max and min}

title: Connectedness
description: When spaces come in one piece

concepts.title: Connected Spaces
concepts.contentHtml:
A space is connected if it cannot be split into two disjoint non-empty open sets. Intuitively, it's "all one piece."

Connected: ℝ, a circle, a torus, any interval [a,b]

Not connected: ℝ \ {0} (the real line with 0 removed splits into positive and negative), two disjoint circles

The connected components of a space are its maximal connected pieces.

concepts.title: Path Connectedness
concepts.contentHtml:
A stronger notion: a space is path connected if any two points can be joined by a continuous path.

Path connected always implies connected, but not vice versa (there are exotic connected spaces with no paths between certain points, though they're hard to visualize).

For "nice" spaces (like subsets of ℝⁿ, manifolds), connected and path connected are the same thing.

concepts.title: The Intermediate Value Theorem (Topologically)
concepts.contentHtml:
The Intermediate Value Theorem from calculus is really a theorem about connectedness:

If f: [a,b] → ℝ is continuous and f(a) < 0 < f(b), then f(c) = 0 for some c between a and b.

Why? Because [a,b] is connected, so f([a,b]) must be connected (continuous images of connected sets are connected). A connected subset of ℝ is an interval, so it contains everything between f(a) and f(b).

This reveals that the IVT is fundamentally about topology, not calculus!
mathExpressions: f \text{ continuous}, \; [a,b] \text{ connected} \implies f([a,b]) \text{ connected (an interval)}

concepts.title: Beyond π₁: Higher Homotopy Groups
concepts.contentHtml:
The fundamental group π₁ detects 1-dimensional holes (loops around tunnels). But what about higher-dimensional holes?

π₂ uses 2-spheres instead of loops — it detects "cavities" (like the inside of a hollow sphere).

π₂(S²) = ℤ (one cavity), π₂(ℝ³) = 0 (no cavities)

Higher homotopy groups π₃, π₄, ... are notoriously hard to compute and contain deep, surprising structure.

concepts.title: Homology: A Computable Alternative
concepts.contentHtml:
Homology groups H₀, H₁, H₂, ... provide a more computable way to count holes of each dimension.

H₀ counts connected components
H₁ counts loops/tunnels (1-dimensional holes)
H₂ counts cavities (2-dimensional holes)

The Betti numbers b₀, b₁, b₂, ... are the ranks of these groups. For a torus: b₀=1, b₁=2, b₂=1.

Remarkably, the Euler characteristic is the alternating sum: χ = b₀ - b₁ + b₂ - ...

concepts.title: Topology in the Real World
concepts.contentHtml:
Algebraic topology has explosive modern applications:

Topological Data Analysis (TDA): Persistent homology reveals the "shape" of data sets — finding clusters, loops, and voids in high-dimensional data.

Materials science: Classifying crystal defects and phase transitions using topological invariants.

Robotics: Configuration spaces of robots are topological spaces; their topology determines what motions are possible.

Quantum computing: Topological quantum computers use braided anyons — the braiding is essentially knot theory!
